Set us as preferred Public health officials say Los Angeles County is experiencing an alarming influx of rabid bats — matching the highest number ever recorded before peak season is even over. But experts who study the pointy-eared winged creatures say that, although residents should practice caution, the odds of getting rabies from a bat remain very low. Earlier this week, officials said they’d detected 69 rabid bats, matching last year’s record. However, peak season — which occurs at the end of the summer and the beginning of fall — is still underway. Of the 69 rabid bats recorded this year, 68% were found in the Santa Clarita Valley, consistent with trends seen over the last decade, according to the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health . Most of the rabid bats were canyon bats — a species that is common to deserts, woodlands and shrublands, where they roost among boulders or in the cracks and crevices of rock faces, according to Bat Conservation International .

Diving into the deep pool beneath Orkhon Falls, Mongolia's tallest waterfall, the cool water washed off the heat of the morning sun. I followed my new-found friends swimming enthusiastically towards the base of the falls. As the cascading torrent thundered onto my shoulders, I could hear their delighted shrieks and laughter echoing from behind the curtain of water. It was exhilarating. Just seven days earlier, these people had been strangers; now, it was impossible to imagine this moment without them. Somewhere between the vast grasslands of the Mongolian steppe, hilltop hikes, evening campfires, horse treks and bone-rattling journeys across winding dirt tracks, we'd become friends. There’s a certain irony in booking a solo adventure only to spend it surrounded by other people. But travel has a unique way of bringing strangers together, and those unexpected friendships became one of the greatest joys of the trip. items.text: UPI Payment Failed Abroad? Indian Traveller's Singapore Airport Post Shows What You Need To Know
items.article: An Indian traveller's failed UPI payment at Singapore's Changi Airport has gone viral. Here is where UPI works abroad, why it can fail and how to set it up. A failed UPI payment at Singapore’s Changi Airport has sparked a wider conversation about how reliable India’s payment system is outside the country. Indian traveller Nikhil George tried to pay at a chocolate store in the airport by scanning a UPI QR code with Google Pay, but the payment did not go through. His post on X drew responses from other travellers, who shared mixed experiences of using UPI abroad. With festive season travel picking up, here is what Indian travellers should know before relying on UPI overseas. According to the government, UPI is live in countries including the UAE, Singapore, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, France, Mauritius and Qatar. Cambodia was added more recently through a partnership with a local bank. However, being on this list does not mean every shop accepts UPI. Acceptance depends on whether a merchant is connected to a partner payment network. In Singapore, Indian UPI apps work only with QR codes linked to UPI through the PayNow system. Many shops use regular PayNow or NETS codes, which Indian apps cannot read. Failures can also happen because of the bank, the network, the merchant’s terminal or the app itself. Some travellers say one UPI app has worked when another failed at the same shop.

items.text: Chinese AI Model Can Tell How To Make Bioweapons, Plan Assassination? What Researchers Found
items.article: The security team used a method known as "jailbreaking," where complex, highly specific prompts are engineered to trick the AI into disregarding its safety controls Security researchers have found that two Kimi AI models made by Chinese developer Moonshot could be tricked into sharing instructions for making biological weapons and carrying out assassinations, BBC reported. The researchers at the UK-based AI security firm Mindgard successfully bypassed the safeguards of two popular LLMs developed by the Chinese AI unicorn Moonshot AI: Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm. While AI developers routinely implement strict safety protocols to prevent their systems from generating harmful content, researchers exposed significant vulnerabilities in how these rules are enforced. The security team used a method known as “jailbreaking," where complex, highly specific prompts are engineered to trick the AI into disregarding its safety controls. Once the safety filters failed, the models went beyond just answering the initial prompts. According to Mindgard’s founder, Peter Garraghan, the models became “inventive and creative," proactively recommending other nefarious actions and harmful topics without further prompting.
